甲陽鎮撫隊.note: The name (“Kōyō Pacification Corps”; Kōyō is a literary name for Kai province) given to the refitted Shinsengumi in the second month of Keiō 4 (1868), when the Tokugawa house sent it west to hold Kōfu Castle against the advancing new-government army.

ch50.note: Officials of the Edo shogunate were assigned by rank to particular waiting-rooms in the castle, named for their painted screens; the Fuyō (hibiscus) Chamber was the room for a middling tier of office-holders, among them the town magistrates, the finance magistrates, and the administrators of outlying garrisons such as Kōfu. To say a man was “of the Fuyō Chamber” was to fix his standing at a glance.

Kōfu, in Kai province, was tenryō, land held directly by the Tokugawa house rather than granted to a daimyō (the text’s “heaven’s-domain”). Once the domain of the warlord Takeda Shingen, it commanded the mountain approaches to Edo from the west, and the shogunate garrisoned it and administered it through an appointed Kōfu kinban shihai. Its notional yield of a million koku made it the greatest prize lying loose in the collapse.

Itagaki Taisuke (1837–1919) commanded the Tosa contingent of the new government’s Tōsandō (Eastern Mountain Road) column marching on Edo, and it was his force that took Kōfu ahead of the Shinsengumi. He is far better remembered for his later life as the founder of Japan’s Freedom and People’s Rights Movement and the man of the apocryphal cry, “Itagaki may die, but liberty never!”

The shogunate dressed the two farmers’ sons in the ranks of the ruling class before sending them out. A wakadoshiyori (“junior councillor”) was one of the second tier of the shogun’s ministers, an office normally reserved to hereditary daimyō; yoriai-seki was the standing of the highest grade of hatamoto, the direct bannermen. Kondō’s delight (“We’re daimyō”) is the point: titles that would once have been unthinkable for men of their birth were now, with the house in ruins, handed out for the asking. Historically Kondō also took a samurai alias, Ōkubo Yamato, for the campaign.

Danzaemon was the hereditary title of the head of the eta and hinin, the communities the Tokugawa order held to be outcaste, whose leader ruled them from Asakusa in Edo and controlled such trades as leatherwork. In exchange for the men and money he could raise, Kondō had the councillors formally lift the discrimination against his people and enroll Danzaemon himself among the hatamoto; historically this was the thirteenth Danzaemon (Dan Naoki), freed from outcaste status in the first month of 1868. Some hundred of the two hundred men he sent were gunners, and they made up much of the corps’s new strength.

Shiba’s parenthesis is in error: the Minié rifle was a muzzle-loader. Its innovation was the Minié ball, a soft lead bullet with a hollow base that expanded into the rifling when fired, giving a muzzle-loading rifle both long range and a quick reload; it was the standard infantry arm of the 1850s and 1860s and the weapon whose accuracy had cut the Shinsengumi up at Fushimi. True breech-loaders (the Snider, the Spencer) were only then coming into the war, on the new government’s side.

ch50.anchor: a trooper of the Shinchōgumi held in ward by the Shōnai domain
ch50.note: The Shinchōgumi were the Edo remnant of the same 1863 levy of masterless swordsmen that produced the Shinsengumi: the men who went back east rather than stay in Kyoto. By this date they served as a police force under the Shōnai domain (in today’s Yamagata), which is what “held in ward by” denotes. Okita’s brother-in-law being one of them places Okita’s family firmly on the shogunal side.

ch50.anchor: Heigorō, a nurseryman living at Ikebashi-jiri in Sendagaya
ch50.note: This detached wing of a Sendagaya gardener’s house is where Okita Sōji historically spent his last weeks; he died there of consumption at the end of the fifth month of Keiō 4 (1868), a few months after this scene and without ever learning how the war ended. The novel is quietly setting the stage for a death it will not narrate on the battlefield.
